chief_complaint: expanding bull's-eye rash after tick bite hiking
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with expanding bull's-eye rash after tick bite hiking. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the expanding ring is a poisonous spider bite or an allergic reaction to a bug he brushed against while hiking.
concerns: He is worried the venom is spreading through his body and will cause chronic joint pain that keeps him from working his construction job.
expectations: He hopes to get a prescription for an antibiotic ointment or pills so the rash clears up before his weekend camping trip.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Lyme Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Lyme Disease: Oral Doxycycline 100mg BID for 10-14 days, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: expanding bull's-eye rash after tick bite hiking

Key HPI features: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with expanding bull's-eye rash after tick bite hiking. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.4C, HR 76, BP 122/78, well-appearing. Single 8cm annular erythematous patch with central clearing on the right posterior thigh, warm but non-tender, no fluctuance. No lymphadenopathy, normal cardiac and neurologic exam. Lyme serology (ELISA with Western blot confirmation) sent, clinical diagnosis made on exam alone given classic erythema migrans.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Lyme Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cellulitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Cardiac symptoms (suggesting carditis) or neurological symptoms.
management_principles: Plan for Lyme Disease: Oral Doxycycline 100mg BID for 10-14 days
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with expanding bull's-eye rash after tick bite hiking. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.4C, HR 76, BP 122/78, well-appearing. Single 8cm annular erythematous patch with central clearing on the right posterior thigh, warm but non-tender, no fluctuance. No lymphadenopathy, normal cardiac and neurologic exam. Lyme serology (ELISA with Western blot confirmation) sent, clinical diagnosis made on exam alone given classic erythema migrans.
reference_soap.assessment: Early localized Lyme Disease (erythema migrans), diagnosed clinically based on the characteristic expanding annular rash with central clearing following tick exposure in an endemic area.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Lyme Disease: Oral Doxycycline 100mg BID for 10-14 days. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Lyme Disease
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Lyme Disease
Implement evidence-based management plan: Oral Doxycycline 100mg BID for 10-14 days

teaching.one_liner: A tick-borne Borrelia burgdorferi infection causing an expanding bullseye rash (erythema migrans) after a tick bite in an endemic area.
red_flags: Cardiac symptoms (suggesting carditis) or neurological symptoms

must_ask.say: Did you notice a tick bite, or have you been hiking recently?
Does the rash look like an expanding ring?
Any joint pain or flu-like symptoms?
How long has the rash been there?

history.answer: I noticed a strange red bull's-eye rash spreading on the back of my right thigh after a hiking trip, and it seems to be getting bigger.
I went hiking in the woods about a week ago, and a few days later I noticed a small red spot that has gradually expanded into a wide ring.
It is only on the back of my right thigh, and I have not seen any other spots or patches on my body.
It looks like a bull's-eye target with a red outer circle and a clearing in the center, about the size of my palm.
It feels slightly warm when I touch it, but it does not itch or hurt at all.
No, it stays continuously in the exact same spot and does not fade away or reappear somewhere else.
No, I have never experienced a skin rash like this before.
I have been feeling unusually tired and slightly warm over the past two days, but I have not had shaking chills or high fevers.
No, my mouth, eyes, and genital area are completely normal with no sores, blisters, or redness.
No, the skin is intact with no peeling, blistering, or dark purple spots.
No, I have not had any swelling of my lips or face, throat tightness, or trouble breathing.
No, I have not started any new prescription drugs, antibiotics, or pain medications.
No, I have not used any new soaps, detergents, lotions, or cosmetics, and no jewelry touches that area.
No, neither my wife nor the friends who went hiking with me have any rashes or symptoms.
I was hiking through tall grass and brush in the woods last weekend, and I found a small tick attached to that exact spot on my thigh the following day.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or hay fever.
My joints feel completely normal with no pain or swelling, and my fingernails look fine.
I applied an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream a couple of times, but it did not make any difference so I stopped.
I am in a long-term monogamous relationship with my wife, and neither of us has had any genital sores or discharge.
No, I have not had any chest pain, fluttering or racing heartbeats, shortness of breath, or dizziness.
No, I have not had any facial drooping, muscle weakness, numbness, severe headaches, or stiff neck.
I thought maybe a spider bit me while I was hiking in the brush, or my body is having an allergic reaction to some insect.
I'm really worried this poison is spreading into my joints and might keep me from working on the job site.
I have no chronic medical conditions and have always been healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I do not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps one or two beers on the weekend.
I work as an office manager and live in a house with my wife.
My parents are alive and healthy, and there is no family history of chronic skin disorders or autoimmune disease.

exam.finding: Temperature 37.4°C, heart rate 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-appearing adult male in no acute distress, alert and oriented.
Single 8-centimeter annular erythematous patch with central clearing on the right posterior thigh, warm to touch, non-tender, with no fluctuance or induration.
Oral mucosa is pink and moist with no aphthae, ulcers, or mucosal enanthem.
Conjunctivae are clear without injection or discharge, and sclerae are anicteric.
No lymphadenopathy palpated in the cervical, supraclavicular, or occipital regions.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, with no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or irregular beats.
Cranial nerves II through XII intact bilaterally, with symmetrical facial expression and no facial nerve weakness.
Supple neck with full flexion, with no nuchal rigidity or meningeal signs.
No swelling, warmth, redness, or joint tenderness in the knees, ankles, or wrists, with full range of motion.
